clue.text: Darwin's crossword, perhaps

definitions.text: Darwin's crossword, perhaps

parts.note: Darwin traced our descent from apes, so the puzzle he might set is a teaser for simians; really it is a spiky Chilean conifer

explanation.surface: A whimsical guess at what sort of puzzle the great naturalist might have enjoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: A puzzle for apes suits Darwin, whose theory linked humans to them; the phrase is the everyday name of the Chile pine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chilean pine got its popular name because its spiny branches would baffle a climbing ape, a fitting brainteaser for the evolutionist.

clue.text: They were consulted and sometimes worked

definitions.text: They were consulted and sometimes worked

parts.words: They were consulted and sometimes worked
parts.note: ancient shrines such as Delphi were consulted for prophecy, and the idiom 'work the oracle' means to pull strings to get one's way

explanation.surface: Something people once went to for advice, and which occasionally did the trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worked' looks like 'functioned', but it alludes to the idiom 'work the oracle'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrines of prophecy were consulted by petitioners, and 'to work the oracle' is an idiom for wangling a result.

clue.text: If Shaw kicked your shins, what would you do ?

definitions.text: If Shaw kicked your shins, what would you do ?

parts.words: If Shaw kicked your shins, what would you do ?
parts.note: the natural retort is to kick the playwright back, and that phrase, run together, is a word for trifles or fancy titbits

explanation.surface: A playful question about retaliating against the playwright Bernard Shaw.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is entirely indirect: the answer is what you would do (kick Shaw), split differently.
explanation.definitionFit: The question's reply, read as one word, is an old term for trinkets or dainty dishes, from French quelque chose.

clue.text: But it doesn't take all this time to read it

definitions.text: But it doesn't take all this time to read it

parts.words: But it doesn't take all this time to read it
parts.note: an annual publication covers twelve months, though reading it takes far less than that

explanation.surface: A reassurance that some lengthy-sounding volume can be read quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: An annual reference volume is named for the twelve-month span it covers, not the time needed to read it.

clue.text: Owing still

definitions.text: Owing still

parts.note: a debt that is still outstanding has not been settled

explanation.definitionFit: A bill that remains owing has not yet been settled by the debtor.

clue.text: A natural exponent of camouflage

definitions.text: A natural exponent of camouflage

parts.note: an animal whose bold stripes are thought to confuse predators practises disguise by nature

explanation.surface: A creature born to disguise itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray '6' is an OCR slip in the printed text.
explanation.definitionFit: The striped African equine's markings are widely cited as natural dazzle camouflage against lions.

clue.text: Get out

definitions.text: Get out

parts.note: to free or disentangle something from a difficulty

explanation.definitionFit: To extricate is to free or release something from entanglement, which is getting it out.

clue.text: "There's Heaven - -,and night by night, I look right through its gorgeous roof " (Browning)

definitions.text: "There's Heaven - -,and night by night, I look right through its gorgeous roof " (Browning)

parts.words: "There's Heaven - -,and night by night, I look right through its gorgeous roof " (Browning)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Robert Browning: the missing word places heaven overhead

explanation.surface: A line of Browning's verse with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Heaven is overhead, so the missing word means higher up or overhead in the line.

clue.text: A ring should be the clue here

definitions.text: A ring should be the clue here

parts.words: A ring should be the clue here
parts.note: a wedding band on the finger signals that someone has a spouse

explanation.surface: A detective's hint that a ring will crack the case.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding band is the giveaway that a person is wed, so the ring is the clue to their state.

clue.text: Fictional careerist

definitions.text: Fictional careerist

parts.note: George Meredith's novel is titled after its hero's career

explanation.definitionFit: Nevil, hero of George Meredith's novel of 1875, has a career that gives the book its title.

clue.text: No doubt a bother to his enemies,-it's a matter of accent

definitions.text: No doubt a bother to his enemies,-it's a matter of accent

parts.words: No doubt a bother to his enemies,-it's a matter of accent
parts.note: the Boer general Louis, later South African premier, troubled the British, and his surname said in a certain accent is 'bother'

explanation.surface: Some troublesome figure annoyed his foes, a matter of how you pronounce it.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis, the Boer commander and first South African prime minister, was a thorn in British sides; his surname spoken with a non-rhotic accent echoes 'bother'.

clue.text: It will solve itself

definitions.text: It will solve itself

parts.note: the letters of 'solve' themselves rearrange into a word for small rodents

explanation.surface: A problem that will sort itself out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solve itself' hints that the letters of 'solve' are rearranged into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The field rodents' name is a rearrangement of 'solve', so the word solves itself.

clue.text: Starting with a ship the soldier takes a mixed ride

definitions.text: soldier

indicators.note: the ship comes at the start of the soldier's name, with the rest following

parts.note: a brig is a two-masted sailing ship

indicators.note: mixed means the letters of ride are jumbled up

explanation.surface: A soldier begins on a ship, then goes for a rough ride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starting with' puts the sailing vessel at the front; 'a ship' together is the two-masted brig, not the article plus a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior army officer above a colonel commanding a brigade is a rank of soldier.

clue.text: Coal's an export of this place

definitions.text: this place

indicators.note: the words are carried away from their home order, so their letters are shipped out and rearranged

explanation.surface: Coal is what this town sends abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'export' looks like trade, but it rearranges the letters of COAL'S AN.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Philistine city on the Levant coast is the place named, Richard I's Crusader stronghold.

clue.text: I will 'not say, pity me; 'tis not a soldier-like (Mer. Wi.)

definitions.text: I will 'not say, pity me; 'tis not a soldier-like (Mer. Wi.)

parts.words: I will 'not say, pity me; 'tis not a soldier-like (Mer. Wi.)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from The Merry Wives of Windsor, where the missing word is an expression or form of words

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare with its last word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: In Merry Wives Bardolph calls 'pity me' an unsoldierly expression, a set form of words.

clue.text: '1 h.p. 3-seater

definitions.text: '1 h.p. 3-seater

parts.note: one horsepower is literally one horse, drawing a two-wheeled carriage carrying two passengers and a driver

explanation.surface: A motoring spec sheet for a tiny, low-powered three-seat car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'h.p.' looks like engine power, but here it is a single real horse.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian two-wheeled carriage had one horse pulling it and seated two passengers plus the driver.

clue.text: Porker among inebriates

definitions.text: Porker among inebriates

indicators.note: among puts the porker within the drunkards

parts.note: sots are drunkards
a porker is a pig

explanation.surface: A pig rooting around in a crowd of drunks.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives only wordplay; the answer, barrel taps, belongs among drinkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Taps on casks are what drunkards gather round, so the picture of a beast among drinkers points to barrel bungs.

clue.text: Falcon which may have a longer tail

definitions.text: Falcon which may have a longer tail

parts.words: Falcon which may have a longer tail
parts.note: the bird's name can be spelt with or without an extra final letter

explanation.surface: A hawk whose tail feathers might be extra long.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Longer tail' means an extra letter at the end of the word, not plumage.
explanation.definitionFit: The fast hunting raptor's name has a variant spelling with an E added at the end.

clue.text: It has a church of its own, but abroad is aspirated capital

definitions.text: It has a church of its own

parts.note: Paris is the capital abroad, in France
aspirating adds a breathed H sound, so H is the letter added

explanation.surface: A district with its own church, which overseas becomes a breathy capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abroad' points to a foreign capital, France's.
explanation.definitionFit: A local ecclesiastical district is served by its own church and clergy.

clue.text: Luck is sometimes measured as such cheese

definitions.text: Luck is sometimes measured as such cheese

parts.words: Luck is sometimes measured as such cheese
parts.note: a stroke of fortune may be called 'a ... of luck', and the run-together phrase is melted cheese on toast

explanation.surface: Fortune can be weighed out like a portion of cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh toasted cheese is called by this name, which also splits into a phrase for an uncommon piece of luck.

clue.text: The bad are said to turn up

definitions.text: The bad are said to turn up

parts.words: The bad are said to turn up
parts.note: the proverb says a bad coin always reappears

explanation.surface: Wicked people are reputed always to reappear.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb 'a bad penny always turns up' refers to small British coins.

clue.text: When a dowry is received ?

definitions.text: When a dowry is received ?

parts.note: dot is French for a dowry, and age means a time or period, so the phrase is jokingly the dowry's time

explanation.surface: A question about the time a bride's portion is handed over.
explanation.definitionFit: Senile old age splits as French 'dot', a marriage portion, plus 'age', a period of time.

clue.text: So far as Mr. Weller was concerned, its contents were " inwariable"

definitions.text: So far as Mr. Weller was concerned, its contents were " inwariable"

parts.words: So far as Mr. Weller was concerned, its contents were " inwariable"
parts.note: in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, Sam Weller's father speaks of drink with his Cockney swap of v for w

explanation.surface: A Dickens character's view that some vessel always held the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: The drinking vessel Mr Weller refers to always held liquor, its 'inwariable' contents in his Cockney speech.

clue.text: It yields golden air

definitions.text: It yields golden air

indicators.note: yields means the letters of golden air give up their order and produce something new

explanation.surface: Something that fills the air with golden light.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotating firework, or a branched candlestick, scatters glittering light into the sky or room.

clue.text: Man like a Cockney horseman

definitions.text: Man like a Cockney horseman

parts.note: a Cockney drops the h, so 'an horseman' slurs into a phrase naming a Viking rider

explanation.surface: Someone who resembles a London rider.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys drop the H, so the article's N slides onto the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney's 'an 'orseman' sounds like 'a Norseman', so the adjective describes a Scandinavian man.

clue.text: "Alas, a black -, cousin Shallow " (2 Henry IV)

definitions.text: "Alas, a black -, cousin Shallow " (2 Henry IV)

parts.words: "Alas, a black -, cousin Shallow " (2 Henry IV)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2, where Silence describes someone dark as a blackbird

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare with a word left out.
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for the blackbird, used in the Shakespeare line to describe a dark-complexioned woman.

clue.text: Tough guy

definitions.text: Tough guy

parts.note: someone who endures hardship without complaint

explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Zeno's philosophy, or anyone who bears pain impassively, is hardy in spirit.

clue.text: It's little and beaten.

definitions.text: It's little and beaten.

parts.note: a small drum is something struck with a stick

explanation.surface: Something small that takes a thrashing.
explanation.definitionFit: The small medieval drum played with one hand is little and is beaten.

clue.text: "The — crime of being a young man "(Pitt)

definitions.text: "The — crime of being a young man "(Pitt)

parts.words: "The — crime of being a young man "(Pitt)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank from William Pitt the Elder's famous retort in the Commons to Walpole

explanation.surface: A quotation from Pitt with its adjective left out.
explanation.definitionFit: Pitt ironically called youth a dreadful, heinous crime, the missing adjective.

clue.text: Two runs, from the striker's point of view

definitions.text: Two runs, from the striker's point of view

parts.words: Two runs, from the striker's point of view
parts.note: in cricket a batsman scoring two runs goes to the far wicket and returns

explanation.surface: A cricket scoring note about a batsman's two runs.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the striker is the batsman facing the bowler; each run is a dash between the two wickets.
explanation.definitionFit: Scoring two in cricket means the batter runs to the opposite crease and returns, a round trip.
